speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether there will be guidelines or criteria developed for the reactivation of TraceTogether and SafeEntry as contact tracing tools; and (b) what examples of future situations where these tools may be used so that the public can take the necessary steps to retain their tokens where necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the pandemic situation stabilised, the Multi-Ministry Taskforce (MTF) took decisive steps to open up social and economic activities to almost pre-COVID-19 norms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, to Ms Sylvia Lim's question, temples can start to organise dinners, barring any changes in rules later.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked if individuals who are not fully vaccinated can be allowed to enter malls and dine in F&B outlets.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we still need to remain cautious because the next infection wave is highly possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will continue to review our VDS measures as the pandemic situation evolves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are taking a cautious "step down but not dismantle" posture for our public health measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the situation requires, we will have to step up VDS and reactivate TraceTogether and SafeEntry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin asked what the criteria are to reactivate these measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a matter of judgement, depending on the severity of the situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will have to take into account if there is a new variant of concern, whether it is more severe or more infectious than the Omicron variant, whether past infections and current vaccines continue to confer strong protection against the new variant and how all these affect our hospital capacity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I can understand that some members of the public and Members of the House want a system, with transparent and clear triggering points, but I am afraid this is not possible when we are in a pandemic crisis with fog of war.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Through MTF's actions over the years, I hope the public would also appreciate where we are coming from.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do what is necessary to protect lives when danger is upon us and we will step down measures when they are no longer needed, no longer necessary, so that people can resume their normal lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the best step for the public to take is not to delete your TraceTogether app and not to throw away your TraceTogether tokens.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members asked about the Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: DORSCON was established after SARS in 2003, then reviewed and progressively improved upon from the experiences drawn from managing the H1N1 pandemic in 2009, and the coordination for the Middle Eastern Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus and Ebola Virus Disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Post-COVID-19, we will, certainly, review it further, along with our response measures, given all that we have learnt during this pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The DORSCON framework was developed as a tool for Ministries and agencies to coordinate and execute the Government's response to outbreaks of infectious diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By and large, it has served its purpose well in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the initial phase of the pandemic, MTF decided that, for transparency, we would announce the DORSCON level and colour code publicly, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This would help alert the public to the need for personal vigilance and social responsibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, it had also led to certain public reactions, such as the rush to the supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is one key issue for review as DORSCON is meant to bolster preparedness, not to induce public anxiety.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A key factor to consider in our review of the DORSCON framework is that after more than two years of the pandemic, the Government and our society have learnt a lot about pandemic response.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have developed a comprehensive response system, covering health protocols, border controls and safe management of social and economic activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is also tiered and differentiated, catering to different activities and settings, such as schools, offices, public spaces, eating places, nightlife, events and so on, with various severity conditions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, from a public communications point of view, we believe that the public now pays much less attention to the DORSCON colour code and takes care to understand the various public health measures in detail, and then respond and do their part accordingly, be it taking vaccination, wearing masks or abiding by the safe management measures (SMMs).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I am confident that today, we have a much more sophisticated public that understands what they need to do when a pandemic turns for the worse.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The response of the public and the contribution of everyone in our society are, ultimately, what give us resilience during a pandemic outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the DORSCON framework is most likely still relevant, but it needs to be part of a larger emergency preparation and public communications framework that we have already developed and people now understand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It means comparing death rates across the years, taking into account the changing age profile of the population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the death rate goes up in a pandemic, above that expected in the absence of a pandemic and over what is expected from population ageing, it means there are excess deaths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, 2021 is about the same as 2017, just a notch lower.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there are excess deaths in 2021, compared to 2020.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Leon Perera asked why that is so and how we calculate excess deaths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We used well-established, internationally-practised methods, including age adjustments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are excess deaths in 2021 because there had been a global pandemic, causing millions of deaths around the world, and Singapore was not exempted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: During a pandemic, excess deaths will be higher than officially reported deaths directly caused by the disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To illustrate, a recent WHO analysis of excess deaths found that while the officially reported number of COVID-19-related deaths around the world is slightly over six million, "excess deaths" during this pandemic is 15 million – about 2.5 times more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are a few reasons to explain the difference in the two numbers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One, in some parts of the world, there can be under-reporting in regions where testing is insufficient or where data is difficult to collate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, in Singapore, this is not an issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Two, there are infected persons who died of other illnesses, where the COVID-19 infection might have been a contributory factor but not the main cause.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, individuals with chronic conditions may put off their check-ups, treatments and medications during the pandemic, to their own detriment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Four, there are many regions where their healthcare systems were overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When that happens, proper care is denied and the people who suffer are not just the COVID-19-infected patients, but everyone who needs hospital care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The remainder excess deaths could be due to some of the factors I explained earlier, except under-reporting, which is not an issue in an urban environment like Singapore; also, the last reason I mentioned, hospitals being overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is not a big factor here, because we prioritised the protection of our healthcare system, going into a circuit breaker when necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, although our hospitals came under significant pressure at the height of the infection waves, they were not overwhelmed, and hospitals could continue to give priority to serious and urgent cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As mentioned in the Ministry of Health (MOH) press release on 24 March 2022, MOH is continuing to collect and analyse the data, particularly the recent Omicron data, to find out more comprehensively the impact of this crisis on Singapore residents and we will release a special report soon to estimate the excess deaths over the past two and half years of the pandemic and the key factors causing the excess deaths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should emphasise that whether it is official COVID-19 death toll or excess deaths, Singapore will have one of the lowest rates in the world, amongst countries that have chosen to live with COVID-19 and resumed normal lives, and that is because of the cooperation of everyone in Singapore and the effectiveness of protecting our healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a supplementary question and it was an article in The Straits Times yesterday, which said, and I quote, "TraceTogether tokens and even SafeEntry Gateway boxes are Government properties and throwing them away could be considered an offence", and it then goes on to list certain offences under the Penal Code, Vandalism Act and Computer Misuse Act.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think, this has caused some alarm among people who may have inadvertently disposed of or misplaced their tokens.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, it will be very helpful to have some clarification on what to do with these tokens and what happens if there has been any inadvertent disposal, as well as some assurance in terms of the data that is or is not connected while the app remains in the phone.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I read the article as well and I thought there might be a supplementary question on it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will need to check with GovTech with regard to the status of all the equipment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for those who have inadvertently disposed of them, do report them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am sure the Government agencies will be as helpful as they can to try to replace them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think our key consideration is not so much about protection of the equipment, but to make sure that should we have another variant of concern, businesses, individuals, we are ready to respond.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned this in an earlier reply, which is, that for events, for example, nightlife with dancing, where SafeEntry data is still collected, it will be purged very quickly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister for Health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He mentioned earlier that vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS) will still be needed for events of more than 500 participants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can he clarify that this also applies to the community dinners that I asked for, meaning that, if the number of participants is expected to be more than 500, then the organisers would have to check that the participants are vaccinated?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, the Minister mentioned that these dinners can proceed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I spoke to some unvaccinated people and they shared that, for many of them, they choose not to be vaccinated because they are worried about the severe adverse reactions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Minister had said that the health care system is not overwhelmed, the majority of Singaporeans are vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, is there any way in which we can really consider removing some of the VDS, so that those who choose not to be vaccinated for whatever reasons can lead their lives as per the rest of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are only about 3.5% of such people and, really, they ought to take responsibility for their own decision not to be vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, we all take responsibility for our own health and make our own decisions regarding our own health status, including vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The issue that we do need to consider here is that, in a pandemic crisis, individual decisions also affect the society and the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When that happens, it is not just the unvaccinated who will suffer, not those who are infected that will suffer, but everyone who requires hospital care, acute care and emergency services will suffer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is because of that, that the decision not to vaccinate yourself is no longer just about yourself; it is also a role for us to protect the whole society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we do worry about the next variant of concern.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most likely, it will evolve and emerge in the months to come.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, given that posture, I think, just maintain these three most risky settings where VDS will still apply and we will continue to review the situation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If I heard correctly, the Minister said he would answer all questions until Question No 13.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am just wondering if he has answered Question No 13 as well, which is about the impact of restraints placed on non-urgent treatments and testing during COVID-19 and what backlog has there been for such treatments and testing, and what has that impact been.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, whether the Ministry will conduct a study on the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on various aspects, as I mentioned, we have issued a Press Statement on 24 March, and said that we will collate all the data, and do a proper study.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a special report on the impact of the entire pandemic and we will answer some of the questions, including the data required.
